Retiring at the age of 60 was so normal but in the recent times, retirement planning conversations are picking up, and we found this comment by a Reddit user quite interesting.
Text within this block will maintain its original spacing when published “I’m a millennial, and to be honest, no one taught us retirement planning. The stage was set: study hard, get a good job, get married, etc...Financial independence and saving for retirement are concepts we’re only learning now.Maybe the next generation will learn faster.”
We’re not surprised reading this, are we?
Most of us didn’t grow up in homes where money, investment, family finances, and retirement were conversations at the dinner table.
Schools never taught us personal finance, and we watched our grandparents being taken care of by their children. So, for the longest time, we never really paid attention to what it deserved.
And it is reflected in various reports. Survey after survey points to the same thing: India is under prepared for retirement.
Let’s look at the current situation. According to government data, around 24 crore Indians will be over the age of 60 by 2041 — that’s everyone aged 44 and above as of today.
Source: Economic Survey 2018-19
Now, look at the investing population in India. We have about 10-12 crore unique demat and mutual fund accounts as of now.
But most of these accounts were opened post-COVID by younger individuals. Only a fraction of them are likely to be held by those above the age of 44.
So, where are the rest investing for their future?
Maybe some are big on real estate. But how many would actually be willing to sell their homes to fund retirement? Perhaps they plan to live off rental income. That’s possible, but how many will find it sufficient?
Others may be investing in traditional debt products like PPF and EPF. But with rising costs, especially expected medical inflation at 13%- 14% (which will hit the elderly hardest), but will that really be enough? Probably not.
And even among those who are investing, how many are doing it specifically with retirement in mind?
We Agree, these are rough, back-of-the-envelope calculations, but it is certainly not exaggerated.
We don’t need extensive reports and surveys to establish the fact that India is not well prepared for retirement .
Unless someone has a large inheritance, starts saving aggressively in their 40s (which requires sacrificing a lot), or has a lifelong pension coming in, many will find it hard to retire on their own terms.
“Earn more and save aggressively — even if it means tough decisions like not having kids or not buying a house… Or maybe one day, I do have kids and just hope they’re as conscientious as I am and support retired parents as my wife and I do.”
Said and another Reddit user seemingly in his early 30s that sounded like a sacrifice for retirement.
If I am not wrong, you must be raising your eyebrows reading this. Sounds extreme at first, but there’s a ring of truth in there.
It’s a no-brainer that if we don’t plan properly, we will likely depend on someone, and that someone would be mostly our children.
And before you say, “I’ll just keep working” , take a moment. Think about the speed at which AI is replacing jobs, and how tough the job market already is for those in their 40s.
Now, one part of his comment that’s genuinely unsettling is the idea of not having kids or not buying a house just to save for retirement.
Is retirement planning supposed to demand that kind of sacrifice?
How much should you save now for retirement?
The table below gives you a rough idea of how much money you’ll need to retire, based on your age and current monthly expenses.
Select the cell that matches your age and monthly expenses. The number in blue font tells the total amount (in crore) you should aim to have by age 60. That amount will allow you to live the way you do now until you're 100.
Right below that, the number in black font tells you how much you need to invest every month via SIP, starting today, to reach that goal.
Let’s say you’re 30 and your monthly expenses are around ₹25,000, You’d need about ₹4.9 crore by the time you hit 60 to keep the current lifestyle going.
To get there, you’d need to invest ₹15,766 every month starting now.
Setting aside ₹15K+ every month at age 30 might work for some, but for many, it’s not that easy. You might already be juggling a home loan, car EMIs, or prioritising the education of your kids.
There’s a way to solve for that. Go for a step-up SIP. Basically, you start with a smaller amount initially and slowly increase it every year.
Step-up SIP
The table below is similar to the first one, just that the number in black font tells you how much you need to invest in the first year if you plan to increase it by 15% consequently.
Going back to our example, if you're okay increasing your SIP by 15% every year, you can start with just ₹3,149/month in year one (instead of ₹15,766) to reach your Rs 5 crore retirement goal.
Next year, you have to invest ₹3,621 per month. Then ₹4,164 in year three, and so on.
By the time you’re 60, your monthly SIP would be around ₹1.8 lakh - but that’s 30 years from now.
So, ask yourself do you (and most of India's working population) really need to sacrifice having kids and a home to invest about ₹3,149 a month to begin with?
(Unless, of course, you’re planning to retire at 40 or have a high-spending lifestyle. That’s a different ball game.)
Calculator
We are sharing a retirement calculator where you can customize based on your own lifestyle and goals - Link
(If you can’t edit, download the file to your system or make a copy of the sheet)
To give you a gist, the calculator takes monthly expenses, adjusts them for inflation, and estimates the total retirement corpus needed to last till life expectancy.
Then, based on the number of years until retirement, it tells you how much you need to invest monthly to hit that goal at a certain return.
Be prepared for retirement
We have always believed that the starting point for retirement planning is to
Know how much you’ll need.
Start investing, even if it’s a small amount.
Calculators are a great starting point. But do remember, the real world rarely behaves like Excel.
One bad market year, and your corpus can shrink faster than expected. So when you key in your numbers, be generous and build a buffer.
Also, the retirement numbers can look big and intimidating at first, but here’s a reminder about the magic of compounding,
At 12% pa, ₹20K SIP takes ~15 years to reach ₹1 crore
But the second crore comes in just 5 years
The third takes 3 years
The next 2 crores? 2.3 years and 1.8 years respectively
So start early and stay invested for the long term. Let time do the heavy lifting so you won’t have to in your old age.

I was surprised by a LinkedIn post that went viral last week. The author of the post says that the new middle class in an Indian metro city is the one with an income of Rs 70 lakh per annum and that “by the end of the month, there's nothing left!!!”
Whether we earn ₹7 lakh or ₹70 lakh a year, with money, it often feels like it’s never enough.
A survey conducted by the World Economic Forum in 2024 found that one of the primary reasons individuals don't invest is that they “don’t have enough money.”
Source: World Economic Forum
While I don’t deny the inflation or higher cost of living in metro cities, I also don’t think the amount you earn can define whether you have enough to invest or not.
I am sure you probably know someone earning just a few thousand rupees a month, managing to save something regularly.
You might have encountered a few others, too, who earn a six-figure income but struggle to set aside money for investments.
For the latter, as per their mental accounting, saving a small amount will not make any major difference. They often wait to earn more to ‘properly’ start investing.
Loss of lost time
Let’s look at the reality for most salaried folks. Our peak earning years typically span from age 35 to 55, though salary jumps tend to slow down after 45.
(That’s assuming AI doesn’t drastically change the game in the coming years.)
Now, imagine two investors:
Investor A delays investing until 40, for whatever reason.
Investor B starts at 30, investing whatever little they can afford.
Even if investor A tries to catch up later by investing twice as much as B, he or she still falls short of what investor B accumulates, simply because of losing a decade of compounding.
In this formula of compound interest -> P × (1 + r)^n
We may not always control P (how much you invest), or r (the returns you get).
But n (time) is completely in your hands. And whether we like it or not, it’s often the single most powerful variable.
The real cost of delay
Now, that person who delays investment might think they'll simply save however much it takes when they start earning more in the future, even if it means sacrificing lifestyle choices.
Sure, it might work out if they're really dedicated. The Excel calculations show it's mathematically possible.
But here's the real question: can they actually pull it off?
As you read this, you and I know there are things in our lives we could be doing better – hitting the gym regularly, maintaining a proper sleep schedule, developing that hobby, or finishing that course to boost our resume. Yet we struggle to stick with these good intentions.
Why? As Daniel Kahneman puts it, "Laziness is built deep into our nature." It requires enormous willpower and self-control to change our old habits and do something new.
Now imagine someone who's gotten used to a certain lifestyle and spending pattern suddenly trying to switch to a saving and investing mindset. That's not just difficult – it's mentally exhausting.
Psychologist Roy Baumeister said -
“Effort of will or self-control is tiring; if you have had to force yourself to do something, you are less able to exert self-control when the next challenge comes around. This phenomenon has been named ‘ego-depletion.”
Think about small instances in our day-to-day routine. After a demanding workday, how much mental energy do you have to convince yourself to hit the gym, or say ‘no’ to your favourite dessert or endless scrolling? Probably not much.
Ditching our diet, overspending on impulsive purchases, and getting easily triggered by someone's comment – these are all signs of ego depletion in action.
Money decisions aren't immune to this. When you're already forcing yourself to save aggressively (which goes against your old habits), how will you react when the market drops?
What happens when you face an unexpected expense, but it means skipping your monthly investment? Or when you have a rough day and think, “What’s the point of all this if I can't even enjoy what I earn?”
“After exerting self-control in one task, you simply don't feel like making an effort in another – even though you could do it if you really had to.”
(From the book - Thinking, Fast and Slow)
That's why the real cost of delaying investment isn't just the wealth you lose to time. But also the habit you never build and the discipline that never becomes second nature.
These qualities come only with time and become nearly impossible to build when we are trying to catch up under pressure.
The point is simple - ‘starting small and early’ can easily beat ‘waiting to invest when you have enough.’
The first place to look for that small amount to invest is to run through our expenses, identify the biggest unnecessary spending, and route that money to investing.
As Warren Buffett said, “The best time to invest was yesterday. The next best time is today.”
